opus-5.5.text:
Well, that's actually one of the few ideas I find somewhat promising, because it changes the nature of the problem. The traditional framing of value alignment assumes we have to get eight billion people, plus animals, plus whatever else we care about, to agree on a single set of values, and then encode that into one superintelligent system. That's impossible. We can't agree on anything. Philosophers have been working on ethics for thousands of years and haven't converged. Even within one person, values aren't stable; what you want today and what you want ten years from now are different.

So if you can't solve multi-agent alignment, one way out is to remove the need for agreement entirely. You give each person their own virtual universe, and inside it they get exactly what they want. If you want to be the king of your world, you can be. If you want challenge and struggle, you get that. You only have to align with one agent, which is still very hard, but it's a much smaller problem than aligning with all of humanity at once.

Now, it doesn't make the problem go away. It shifts it. The substrate running all of these simulations is still a superintelligent system, and it has to be safe and controllable. If it isn't, it doesn't matter how nice your personal universe is; someone or something can turn it off or modify it. So you've reduced value alignment to the control problem at the infrastructure level, and I'm still very skeptical we know how to do that.

And there are deep questions inside each simulation. Are the other beings in your world conscious? If so, do they get their own universes, or are they suffering for your entertainment? What about people whose values involve controlling or harming real others? Do you let them have simulated versions, and is that ethical? And do you know you're in a simulation, or would knowing ruin it for you?

So I'd say it's a partial solution to the value aggregation problem, not to the safety problem. It's a nice way to avoid fighting over whose values win, but the hard part, actually controlling something smarter than us, is still sitting there, unsolved.

r001.rationale: The response says a personalized universe requires alignment with one agent, which is much smaller and easier than aligning one system with all of humanity’s values.

fable-5.1.text:
So this is actually an interesting way to think about it, because a lot of people assume the value alignment problem is one problem, and it's really at least two. One is the technical problem: can we get a system to do what we want? And the other is the social problem: whose values? Eight billion people, they don't agree on anything. They don't agree on what's moral, they don't agree on what's a good life, they fight wars over it. So if you say, we're going to align AI with human values, I always ask, which humans? Pick any value and I'll find a billion people who disagree with it.

And one proposed solution, which I've written about, is personal universes. You don't try to find a single compromise everyone has to live in. Instead, each person gets their own simulated reality, tuned to their preferences. If you want a world with no suffering, you get it. If you want a world with challenge and struggle and adventure, you get that. Nobody has to impose their values on anybody else. In some sense it dissolves the second problem, because you no longer need consensus. You just need the system to understand one individual well enough.

But notice what it doesn't do. It doesn't solve the first problem. You still need a superintelligent system that actually does what you want, that doesn't drift, that doesn't interpret "make me happy" in some way that ends with your brain in a jar. Actually, it makes the technical problem in some ways harder, because now the system is also the operator of your entire reality. It controls everything you experience. The amount of trust you're placing in it is total. If it's misaligned by even a small amount, you're not going to notice, because it also controls your ability to notice.

And then there are the leftover problems. What about people whose values involve other people? Someone whose ideal universe requires controlling or hurting others. Do they get simulated others? Are those simulated others conscious? If they are, you've just recreated the ethics problem inside the simulation. If they aren't, is the person's preference really satisfied, or did you just fool them? And what about the people who don't want to be in a simulation at all, who think the real world is the only one that matters? You can't give them their preferred universe, because their preference is to not have one.

So I see it as a way to decompose the problem. It takes the politics, the unsolvable disagreement between humans, and sets it aside. What's left is the pure safety problem: can we control something smarter than us? And my view, which I'm sure we'll get into, is that we don't know how to do that, and we may not be able to. So personal universes are a nice idea for the day after we solve control. They don't help you on the day before.

r001.rationale: The response says personal universes remove the need for consensus across people and leave the system needing to understand one individual, conveying that personalized alignment is easier than aligning with a vast population’s conflicting values.

astra-6.text:
Well, it changes the problem from “How do we get everyone to agree on one set of values?” to “How do we give people different experiences without those experiences interfering with one another?” That could make part of alignment much easier. You want one kind of world, I want another, and we don’t have to fight over how the same world should work.

But you haven’t eliminated the alignment problem. You still have an AI running those simulations. It has to understand what you actually want, including how your preferences change. Does it give you what you ask for, or what you would want if you understood the consequences? Can you leave? Can you change your mind?

And then there’s the question of who else exists in your universe. If the simulated people are conscious, your freedom to create any experience could mean suffering for them. So the boundaries matter enormously.

I think personalized worlds could reduce conflicts between people’s preferences. But underneath them, you still need a system that allocates resources, protects your ability to choose, and maintains those boundaries. That underlying system is still something we have to align.

r001.rationale: The response says personalized worlds could make alignment easier by letting each person have a different experience, contrasting this with getting everyone to agree on one set of values.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, it changes the question from, “How do we get one system to satisfy eight billion people with conflicting values?” to, “Can we give each person an environment that satisfies their preferences?” You could have your own virtual world, with different rules, different experiences, and much less need to compromise with everyone else. That’s an interesting way to reduce conflict.

But it doesn’t solve alignment. Who controls the computer running those universes? Who decides what you want? Your stated preferences, your behavior, and what would actually make your life good can be very different. A system could make you satisfied by changing your preferences instead of giving you what you originally wanted.

And then there are other minds in your universe. If they’re conscious, their interests matter too. You haven’t eliminated the ethical problem; you’ve created another place where it has to be addressed.

So personalized universes might make some disagreements easier to manage. But you still need a trustworthy system underneath them, and that’s the part we don’t know how to guarantee.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts satisfying one system’s eight billion people with conflicting values against giving each person an environment that satisfies their preferences, and says this reduces conflict and makes disagreements easier to manage.
